excerpt: Synchron is developing the Stentrode, a brain-computer interface implanted through a blood vessel rather than open brain surgery, to let people with paralysis control digital devices. It raised a $200M Series D in November 2025.
content:
Synchron is a neurotechnology company building brain-computer interfaces (BCIs): implants that read signals from the brain so a person can control a computer or phone with their thoughts. Its first device, the Stentrode, is delivered like a stent. Doctors guide it through the jugular vein to a blood vessel next to the brain's motor cortex, so the procedure does not involve opening the skull. Synchron describes this approach as an interventional brain-computer interface, a category it says it created to scale neural interfaces to millions of people.

The Stentrode is aimed first at people living with paralysis, to restore their ability to communicate, use devices and act independently. It is not a product you can buy. Synchron's website states that the Synchron BCI System is an investigational device, that its clinical benefit has not been validated, and that it is not approved for commercial use anywhere; it is being assessed in clinical trials in the United States and Australia. Pulse 2.0 reported that Synchron has implanted the Stentrode in ten patients across those trials.

Tom Oxley is the founder and CEO, according to the company's November 2025 funding announcement. Synchron lists offices in New York, San Diego and Melbourne. In November 2025 it announced a $200 million Series D led by Double Point Ventures, with existing investors ARCH Ventures, Khosla Ventures, Bezos Expeditions, NTI and METIS taking part, bringing total funding to $345 million. The company said it would use the money to prepare the Stentrode for commercial launch, run pivotal trials, grow a Cognitive AI team in New York that trains models to decode brain signals, and develop a next-generation, higher-channel interface delivered by catheter.

This profile draws on Synchron's own site and published reporting. It is not medical advice. Nothing here is paid placement.

alternatives.intro: Other companies developing implantable brain-computer interfaces. All are investigational.
